newsitem.title: MEXICO: Populist Cardenas set for victory in Mexico City race.
newsitem.headline: Populist Cardenas set for victory in Mexico City race.

text.p: Leftist veteran Cuauhtehmoc Cardenas, heading for victory in a historic election race for Mexico City mayor, will run the polluted capital with a populist hand if his years as governor of Michoacan are anything to go by.

Here in this small Purepecha Indian village in the heart of western Michoacan state, restored land rights, paved roads, a new school and even indoor toilets are the legacy of Cardenas' efforts as governor to rid his subjects of the shackles of poverty.
Modest measures like these earned Cardenas the enduring support of many here after his 1980-1986 stint at the helm of this predominantly avocado-growing and forestry state.
Nevertheless, to his detractors Cardenas' populist measures were short-term fixes that gathered votes but did little to drive lasting development in the state.

"He came to ask us what we wanted, and we started talking. You can see what he did after that," said Jose Prodigios de Jesus, a mat weaver, pointing out some of the signs of progress that had since fallen into disrepair.

Opinion polls last week showed Cardenas, the son of a former president, with a 20 percentage point lead for the left-leaning opposition Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) in the first Mexico City mayor race in modern history.
Besides that race, Mexico will vote on July 6 to renew the entire lower house of Congress, one-quarter of the Senate and six state governors.
Victory in the capital would give Cardenas a national profile that eluded him in two failed shots at the presidency in 1988 and 1994.

He governed Michoacan as a member of the all-powerful Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled Mexico for 68 years, but left the PRI in disgust in 1988 and is considered by his former cronies a traitor to the party.

"Cardenas led a populist administration. There was a lot of pressing the flesh, but no overall development plan," Arturo Alvarez, a political commentator on local radio and long-standing PRI member, told Reuters.

Cardenas' right-wing opponents have accused him of leading a corrupt administration in Michoacan, during which they alledged he stole public property and gave it to his mother. He has strongly denied the charge.

In the state, locals said the corruption charges were given scant credence. Instead they remembered Cardenas as a steady hand on the tiller, if an uncharismatic leader, who occasionally showed an iron will -- for example, when he closed the red-light district in the state capital Morelia.

"Many housewives used to have nothing, their husbands spent everything (in brothels) on pay day ... Cardenas was a good friend of the people," said Manuel Guevara, a shoe shiner for 49 years on the state capital Morelia's main square.

In the current race, Cardenas has pledged to clamp down on corruption in the police force, tackle suffocating pollution and cut crime in one of the world's largest and most environmentally fragile cities.
If he wins, he will have to work with or against President Ernesto Zedillo -- a zealous political opponent -- and a police chief appointed by Zedillo.

Past experience in Michoacan, where analysts said he squabbled with the central government over budget allocations to the state, suggested he would be neither a willing partner nor a push-over opponent, even though he has pledged not to cast the first stone.
"Is he going to try to be an alternative president? Will he reject a police chief appointed by the president?" Alvarez said.
"Cardenas has seen government. We will see if that has vaccinated him against future mistakes," he added.
